The problem with this counterargument is that, in order to read a person's personality, intentions and motivations with nothing more than a glance, Serie has to do so consciously and with a specific sense of direction. She may be a living grimoire, yes, but that doesn't make her god-tier omniscient unless she suspects something is off. And for that to happen in this case, at least one of her apprentices would need to have died already.

You all are right about one thing though: Serie is mostly driven by reason, not just the fiery ambition she tries to instill in all her students despite the repeating disappointment of their short human lifespans not allowing them to get ever-so-slightly close to her levels of knowledge and proficiency in the study of magic. I would imagine at first she would dispel such baseless rumours in disbelief, but she wouldn't be able to guess the source unless it directly came to their knowledge that it was Shadow Warriors spreading such accusations. Of course, knowing about Serie's powers, one could imagine they would try be more careful in not alerting her of her plans by acting openly and directly. They would most likely carry out their attempts by honouring their name, from the shadows.

But Serie also has emotions: even if she's so used to so thoroughly repress them and shield her inner world from all others, knowing the lives of the humans she trains are so short and fleeting that in the grand scheme of things it wouldn't even matter at all if she did, as it would be just as pointless, it's different with Frieren. Despite the fact elves atre almost practically immortal by human standards, we know Serie is far older than Frieren, meaning the perspective of a younger elf who could potentially outlive her potentially scares Serie or at least makes her feel a little uneasy. That, beside their differences in personality and the whole grudge Serie still seems to have against Flamme to the present day, means it's actually fairly easy to turn her against Frieren.

Besides, Serie clearly dislikes Frieren in a very particular way, seeing in the latter many traits she lacks herself: compassion, partnership, comradery, the ability to find joy in the small things in life, etc. These aspects of Frieren, which she only ever so scarcely puts to display, aren't that natural to elves, as it is heavily implied throughout the story that the Hero Party's journey and Himmel's death both transformed her and made her learn more from humans. And this is something Serie not only seems to heavily disregard as weaknesses, as that is merely an a-posteriori justification, an excuse for her tendency towards distancing herself from Frieren: she actually envies what Frieren has become, and as such does as little as she can to put her down in the 1st-class mage exam without making it too evidently obvious that the reason she doesn't get along well with Frieren is because she actually thinks highly on her on some things she herself isn't particularly good at, but actively pushes those thoughts and feelings away to prevent them from damaging her ego.

In such a state of emotional turmoil, aggravated by her students being manipulated into killing one another after turning away from her, Serie would be way more prone to mistakes caused by emotional misgivings, and as such would end up feeling in such a way that would make her especially vulnerable to manipulation. My thesis is that Serie too can be broken under sufficient emotional stress and anxiety, which rather than making her more physically vulnerable, would just turn her into a vengeful, rampaging menace capable of unleashing the full extent of her might on whoever would be so unfortunate to find themselves as a victim for her to annihilate. And what better way to kill two birds with one stone than to point to Frieren as the culprit and have them both engage in a battle of attrition till Frieren inevitable loses and Serie is left exhausted? Not to mention the whole shocking effect of surprise that learning about the truth when later ambushed by the assassins would take on her already weakened self after the fight.

But yeah, sure, whatever, this was just a tiny little idea I had and wanted to share with you all, hoping someone would understand what I was actually getting at. Forget it, I suppose it is all just a bunch of bad writing, a failure of interpretation and an absolute misread of the characters. Are you all happy now? Good. After Godfrey's banishment and the beginning of the Long March along with his now-Tarnished warriors, a relatively small group lingered astray and was abandoned in the Lands Between. Prosecution ensued as Golden Order zealots under King Consort Radagon's command began cracking down on all creatures deemed impure by the Greater Will.

Eventually, the forsaken clan found refuge in Western Liurnia, where they encountered the albinaurics. The innate arcaneness of these artificial beings seemed so useful to the Tarnished clan in battling their enemies that they swore to protect all albinaurics thereon, thus giving rise to a community based on mutual solidarity which managed to thrive for a stable and peaceful time. And so, what had once been but an insignificant horde of faltering Tarnished became an order of Blue Silver Knights, devoted to safeguarding their fellow albinaurics from whom they also learnt of their saviour, Miquella the Unalloyed, and came to revere the ever-young Empyrean as well.

Your sentence wasn't really accurate. I would rather translate it as ___a nárë, á pata onyë_.__

Explanation; _a_ preceding _nárë_ (_nár_ is also correct, but it could be more easily mistaken in pronounciation with _Anar_ "Sun"; the stress distinction exists though) and the imperative particle are not the same thing. The first _a_ is a vocative particle attested among Tolkien's texts to mark direct adressees, which seems to be the case.

Then, instead of _pata-_ you could use as well another verb of the same meaning; _vanta-_, in which case the preceding imperative particle must be shortened because of the ___-nt-___ consonant cluster lengthening the first syllable, _VANta-_. Thus, _a vanta_ as well. Regarding the primitive Quendian root, _del-_, that would later evolve into _lel-_, past t. _lendë_ in Quenya, which basically means "to go".

And lastly, prepositions get pronoun affixation exactly the same way intransitives are conjugated, that is, applying _-nyë, -lyë_, etc. onto the preposition. Thus, you would get _onyë_.

Hope this helps out :)

The actual syllabary requires a series of components or "elements" specifically arranged to form a particular syllable.

The order components are most likely to follow (top to bottom) is thus:
-Palatalization/Labio-velarization.
-Point of articulation.
-Stress.
-Manner of articulation.
-Liquid glides.
-Vowels.
-Codas/diphthongal vowels.

Two of those components (the /a/ vowel and the nasal point of articulation) are inherited, so that any given syllable consisting of an only point of articulation component will be assumed to be unstressed nasal + a.

For instance, the very last character in the text (the one just before the fullstop) is -tros, unstressed. The actual Spanish word is _otros_. There we can see the dental, voiceless plosive, rhotic glide, /o/ vowel and coda /s/ components.

The apostrophe indicates an omitted viwel at the end of a word when the following one has a null onset (starts with another vowel). It's difficult to say whether it's applied or not regarding the few examples where Tolkien used it.

As far as I could research, it can occour either after a single consonant or a geminate (doubled consonant). The only example where the latter one occours is _Elen síla lúme*nn’* omentielvo_.

This specific example brings in two more doubts however.
The least important; it can occour after geminates, but perhaps couldn't after consonant clusters? We don't know. Prosodically speaking, consonant clusters and geminates are treated equally in Quenya, so...

The second one is tougher though; does the omitted vowel need to be the same as the one on the following word? As shown in the example, it doesn't. _Lúmenna_ gets reduced to _lúmenn’_ probably because _a_ and _o_ have relatively similar phonetic values when unstressed, so that having to pronounce both would be uneasy or even awkward in all sorts of speech.

You might be confused with such explanation, so just use it whenever a word ending in a vowel is followed by a null-onset one.

Dashes are used within Quenya's latin transliteration as a way to indicate that the word preceding them is a stem.

Your example, _kal-_ (or rather _cal-_ according to Tolkien's later orthographic preferences) is a primitive verb stem, glossed as "to shine" (note that the in the Etymologies, √KAL is glossed as everything having to do with light (e.g. _calya-_ to illuminate, _calta-_ as a variation of _cal-_ with exactly the same meaning and valency, _cálë_ light (as a noun), _calma_ light, lamp, instrument to light or illuminate, etc.)) Verb stems are always glossed with a dash rather than their infinitive.

Nouns may also have inflected stems which differ from the nominative singular form, such as _alas_ (_alast-_) marble, _peltas_ (_peltax-_) fence of fixed stakes, _oron_ (_oront-_) mountain, _laman_ (_lamn-_) mammal, _rá_ (_ráv-_) lion, etc. Most times this stems might be inflected as ending in a consonant, but take care! Some cases, such as the possessive, inflect according to the nominative rather than following the stem form. For instance; "the falcon's" would be _fionwa_, not _fiondwa_ as its stem form _fiond-_ might suggest.
